title: Security Awareness Essentials
summary: How attackers actually reach people, what those attempts look like, and the habits that stop them. No jargon, no technical background needed.

lessons.title: Security Awareness Training
lessons.narration:
Welcome. Over the next few minutes we're going to talk about something that touches every person here — security.

Not the technical kind that lives inside firewalls and servers. The everyday kind that lives in your inbox, on your phone, at your desk, and in the small decisions you make without thinking twice.

You don't need a technical background to follow this. There's no jargon and no code. What you will get is a clear picture of how attackers actually try to reach us, what those attempts look like in real life, and the simple habits that stop them.

Consider what these have in common: eighty-one million dollars stolen from Bangladesh's central bank. A fuel pipeline serving America's east coast shut down for six days. The lights going out across two provinces of Ukraine in the middle of winter. In every one of those cases, the entry point was ordinary. An email. A password. A remote-access account nobody had switched off.

Here's what's worth remembering before we start. Attackers rarely break in through technology anymore. They walk in through people — through a rushed click, a reused password, a helpful answer given to the wrong person.

That doesn't make you the weak link. It makes you the control that works. Let's begin.

lessons.title: Why Security Matters
lessons.narration:
Let's start with the honest answer to a fair question: why should this matter to you?

Because the information you handle every day has value to someone else. Customer records. Financial data. Operational systems. Your own login credentials. To an attacker, all of it is either something to sell, something to hold hostage, or a door into something bigger.

In February 2016, attackers who had spent months quietly inside Bangladesh Bank's network issued fraudulent SWIFT payment instructions and moved eighty-one million dollars out of the country. They had even tampered with the bank's printer so the confirmation slips wouldn't appear. They attempted close to a billion dollars in total. What stopped the rest wasn't a security tool — it was a bank employee at a correspondent bank noticing a spelling mistake in one of the instructions.

The consequences aren't abstract. A single compromised account can halt services people depend on, expose personal data belonging to customers and colleagues, and trigger regulatory action and lasting reputational damage.

And it isn't only the organisation's problem. The same habits that protect your work protect your bank account, your family photos, your identity.

Good security at work makes you safer everywhere. That's why it matters.

lessons.title: Phishing Emails
lessons.narration:
Phishing is still the most common way attacks begin — and it works because it doesn't look like an attack. It looks like an email.

Look at three things every time.

First, the sender. It may display a name you recognise, but the actual address behind it is often subtly wrong — an extra letter, a different domain, a public mail service where a company address should be.

Second, the tone. Phishing runs on urgency. Your account will be suspended. Payment is overdue. Act within the hour. That pressure is deliberate. It's designed to stop you thinking and start you clicking.

Third, the links. Hover your cursor over any link and read where it actually goes. The text on screen and the real destination are often two different places.

In December 2015, attackers took down parts of Ukraine's power grid — the first confirmed cyberattack to cause a blackout. Thirty substations went dark and around two hundred and thirty thousand people lost power. It began months earlier with spear-phishing emails carrying an infected Office attachment. Someone opened the file and enabled macros. That single click gave attackers the foothold they used to steal credentials and eventually operate the breakers themselves.

Slow down. Urgency is the attacker's tool, not yours.

lessons.title: Phishing Red Flags
lessons.narration:
Let's turn that into a mental checklist you can run in about ten seconds.

Suspicious sender. Was this expected? Do I know this person, and is the address genuinely theirs? A familiar display name is not proof of anything.

Urgent tone. Am I being pushed to act immediately, or warned that something bad happens if I don't? Genuine business rarely arrives with a countdown attached.

Strange links. Does the destination match the sender? A message claiming to be from your bank shouldn't send you to an unrelated domain. Hover first, click second.

Unexpected attachments. Invoices you never ordered. Delivery notices for parcels you aren't expecting. Documents demanding you enable content before they'll open.

Two patterns show up constantly in Indian workplaces. The first is the fake IT notice: "Your mailbox password expires today — click here to keep your account active." The link opens a perfect copy of your login page, and your credentials go straight to the attacker. The second is invoice fraud: a supplier you genuinely deal with emails to say their bank account has changed, and the next payment goes to a criminal. For any payment-detail change, stop and verify by phone on a number you already hold — never a number in the email.

Any one red flag deserves a second look. Two or more — stop, don't click, and report it.

lessons.title: Password Best Practices
lessons.narration:
Passwords are still the front door to almost everything you use, so let's cover what actually works.

Length beats complexity. A long passphrase of several unrelated words is far harder to crack than a short password stuffed with symbols — and much easier to remember. Aim for at least twelve to sixteen characters.

Never reuse passwords across accounts. This is the big one. Breaches happen constantly, and when credentials leak, attackers immediately try that same combination everywhere else.

In May 2021, the Colonial Pipeline — which carries nearly half the fuel consumed on America's east coast — shut down for six days. Petrol stations ran dry across several states. The entry point was a single password on an old remote-access account that nobody had disabled and that had no second factor. Investigators found that password in a batch of leaked credentials from an unrelated breach, which suggests it had been reused somewhere else. One reused password, on one forgotten account, stopped a pipeline.

Use a password manager. It generates strong, unique passwords for every site and remembers them all, so you only need to recall one strong master passphrase. That's not a shortcut — it's the practical way to do this properly.

And never share your password. Not with a colleague, not with IT, not with anyone who asks.

lessons.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
lessons.narration:
Even a strong password can be stolen. Multi-factor authentication is what makes that theft useless.

The idea is simple. Instead of proving who you are with one thing, you prove it with two. Something you know — your password. And something you have — your phone, an authenticator app, or a hardware key.

An attacker on the other side of the world may have your password. But without that second factor in your pocket, they still can't get in.

Return to Colonial Pipeline for a moment. The compromised account had a password but no second factor. Investigators were explicit that multi-factor authentication on that one legacy account would very likely have stopped the whole incident. It is genuinely that decisive.

Two things to keep in mind. Prefer an authenticator app or a security key over text messages where you have the choice — SMS codes can be intercepted or redirected through SIM-swap fraud.

And treat unexpected prompts as a warning. Attackers now deliberately spam approval requests at all hours, hoping you'll tap "approve" just to make the buzzing stop. That technique has breached major companies. If a prompt appears that you didn't trigger, deny it and report it. Someone already has your password.

lessons.title: Safe Web Browsing
lessons.narration:
The web is where a lot of trouble starts, but a few habits keep you clear of most of it.

Check the address bar. Read the actual domain name carefully, especially the part just before the first slash. Attackers register lookalike domains with swapped letters, extra words, or unusual endings, and they look convincing at a glance.

Look for the padlock and HTTPS — but understand what it means. It tells you the connection is encrypted. It does not tell you the site is honest. Criminals get certificates too.

Be sceptical of pop-ups. Warnings that your device is infected, prizes you've won, urgent prompts to install a plugin — these are bait. Close the tab; don't interact with the pop-up.

Attackers targeting the energy sector have used a technique called a watering hole: rather than attacking a utility directly, they compromise a website that utility staff visit often — an industry association, a trade publication, an equipment supplier's site — and plant malware there. You visit a site you have used for years, and it infects you. Campaigns against energy companies in the US and Europe worked exactly this way.

And avoid downloading software from unofficial sources. Free rarely is.

lessons.title: Social Engineering
lessons.narration:
Social engineering is the art of hacking people instead of systems. It works because it targets instincts that normally serve you well — helpfulness, respect for authority, and the wish to avoid conflict.

Pretexting is the invented backstory. Someone calls claiming to be an auditor, a vendor engineer, or a new colleague on a deadline. The story is plausible, detailed, and completely false.

Impersonation is the borrowed identity. They pose as your manager, your IT team, or a senior executive — usually someone you'd hesitate to question.

Manipulation is the pressure applied on top. Flattery, urgency, sympathy, or mild intimidation, all aimed at getting you to skip the step where you verify.

In September 2023, attackers brought a major international hotel and casino group to a standstill for days. No malware was needed for the first step. They found an employee's details on LinkedIn, telephoned the IT service desk, impersonated that employee convincingly enough to have the credentials reset, and walked in. One phone call. The eventual cost ran into hundreds of millions of dollars.

Your defence is simple and never gets old. Verify independently. Hang up, look up the number yourself, and call back. Genuine requests survive verification.

lessons.title: Vishing and Smishing
lessons.narration:
Phishing doesn't stay in your inbox. It comes by phone and by text too.

Vishing is voice phishing — a live call. The caller may claim to be from your bank, your IT helpdesk, a government office, or a delivery company. They often know a few real details about you, which makes the rest sound true. They may spoof a genuine number on your screen. Caller ID proves nothing.

Smishing is the text-message version. A short SMS or WhatsApp message with a link. A failed delivery. A blocked payment. A refund waiting for you.

One scam is worth naming because it impersonates our own industry. Across India, people receive an SMS reading roughly: "Dear customer, your electricity will be disconnected tonight at 9:30 pm because your previous bill was not updated. Please contact our officer immediately." Victims call the number, are talked into installing a remote-access app to "complete the payment," and their bank account is emptied. Our customers receive these. So do we. If anyone asks you to install an app so they can see your screen, that call is an attack.

The rules are the same in both cases. Never share passwords, one-time codes, or card details with someone who contacted you. Hang up, then reach out yourself on a number you already trust.

lessons.title: What Is Ransomware?
lessons.narration:
Ransomware is malicious software with one purpose: to take your data hostage.

It usually arrives quietly — through a phishing attachment, a malicious link, or a compromised remote-access account. Once inside, it starts encrypting files. Documents, spreadsheets, databases, shared drives. Anything it can reach. Then the demand appears: pay us, in cryptocurrency, within a deadline, and we'll give you the key.

Modern ransomware goes further. Before locking anything, attackers usually copy your data out first. So even organisations with perfect backups face a second threat — publish or sell what we stole unless you pay. That's called double extortion.

In March 2019, the Norwegian aluminium producer Norsk Hydro was hit. Twenty-two thousand computers across forty countries were encrypted in hours. Staff ran plants from paper printouts and whiteboards; some smelters were operated manually to stop the molten metal solidifying. Recovery cost around seventy million dollars. And in November 2022, AIIMS Delhi lost its systems for close to two weeks — appointments, admissions and reports all reverted to paper across one of India's largest hospitals.

The impact is immediate and physical. Systems stop, operations halt, recovery is measured in weeks. Which is exactly why the everyday habits in this training matter. Prevention is dramatically cheaper than recovery.

lessons.title: Ransomware: What To Do
lessons.narration:
If you ever suspect ransomware on your machine, three actions matter — in this order.

One: disconnect from the network. Unplug the network cable and switch off Wi-Fi immediately. This limits how far the encryption can spread to shared drives and other systems. But do not power the machine off — valuable evidence lives in memory, and shutting down destroys it.

Two: report immediately. Call the security team or the helpdesk straight away. Minutes genuinely matter. And never delay because you're worried about being blamed. Fast reporting is what limits the damage, and nobody is penalised for raising the alarm.

Three: do not pay, and do not negotiate. That decision isn't yours to carry alone.

Two contrasting responses are instructive. Colonial Pipeline paid roughly four point four million dollars — and then found the decryption tool the criminals supplied was so slow that they restored from their own backups anyway. Norsk Hydro refused to pay, rebuilt from backups, and did something unusual: they published daily updates, held open press briefings, and told the world exactly what had happened. They were widely praised, kept their customers' trust, and recovered their reputation intact. Transparency turned out to be a better strategy than payment.

Disconnect. Report. Step back and let the response team work.

lessons.title: Physical Security
lessons.narration:
Not every attack arrives over the network. Some walk through the door.

A clean desk is a security control. Documents left out, notes with credentials on them, unlocked drawers — all readable by anyone passing your desk, including cleaners, contractors and visitors. Lock papers away, and lock your screen every time you step away. Every time.

Tailgating is when someone follows you through a secured door without badging in. It feels rude to stop them — which is precisely why it works. Holding a door open for a stranger is not politeness; it's an access-control bypass. Let the door close, and ask them to badge in.

Penetration testers hired to test physical security report success rates that should worry all of us. The standard techniques are embarrassingly simple: carry a large box so someone opens the door for you; wear a high-visibility jacket and carry a clipboard; arrive at the smoking area at shift change and walk back in with the group; or simply say "I've left my badge at my desk." In test after test, these work — not because staff are careless, but because people are decent and don't want to cause a scene.

Wear your badge visibly. If you see someone unfamiliar in a restricted area, ask, or report it.

lessons.title: Remote Work Security
lessons.narration:
Working away from the office removes protection you never noticed you had. Here's how to put it back.

Use the VPN. When you're outside the office, it's what encrypts your traffic and keeps access to company systems controlled. Connect first, then start working.

Lock your screen — always. At home, in a café, at a co-working desk. One second, and it prevents a whole category of problems.

Secure your home Wi-Fi. Change the default router password, use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption, and keep the router firmware updated. Your home network is now part of the company's attack surface.

Remote access is not a small door — for many major breaches it has been the only door. The Colonial Pipeline shutdown started on a dormant VPN account. Attacks on water utilities have begun with remote-support tools left running with shared passwords. The pattern repeats because remote access is convenient, easily forgotten, and rarely reviewed. If you have access you no longer use, tell IT so it can be removed. Unused access is pure risk with no benefit.

And mind your surroundings. Be aware of who can see your screen or hear your calls in shared spaces. Confidential conversations deserve a closed door.

lessons.title: Public Wi-Fi Risks
lessons.narration:
Free Wi-Fi is convenient. It's also uncontrolled, and you have no idea who else is on it or who set it up.

The main risk is interception. On an open network, an attacker sitting nearby can potentially watch unencrypted traffic or position themselves between you and the site you're visiting.

There's a second trick worth knowing: the evil twin. An attacker sets up a hotspot with a name that looks official — the café's name, the airport's name, the hotel's name, something close enough that nobody looks twice. Your phone connects, often automatically if it has seen a similar name before, and everything you do passes through their equipment. The hardware to do this costs less than a decent dinner and fits in a pocket. Journalists and researchers demonstrate it at airports and conferences routinely, harvesting credentials in minutes. So verify the exact network name with staff before joining — and turn off automatic connection to open networks on your phone.

Two rules keep you safe. Always use the VPN on public Wi-Fi. And avoid sensitive tasks — banking, payments, confidential work — unless that VPN is running.

When in doubt, use your mobile hotspot. It's far safer than any open network.

lessons.title: USB and Removable Media
lessons.narration:
A USB stick looks harmless. It can be anything but.

Never plug in a device you didn't buy or weren't issued. Found drives are a genuine attack technique — left in car parks, reception areas, or corridors, relying on curiosity to do the rest. Some are simply infected. Others are engineered to imitate a keyboard and type malicious commands the moment they're connected.

The most consequential example in history is Stuxnet. Around 2010, malware was discovered inside Iran's uranium enrichment facility at Natanz — a site with no internet connection at all, deliberately air-gapped from the outside world. The malware got in on a USB drive, carried across that gap by a person. It then quietly altered the speed of the centrifuges while showing normal readings on the operators' screens, and destroyed roughly a thousand of them before anyone understood why. An air gap is not a wall. It is a wall with a door, and USB devices are the door.

If you must use removable media, scan it first, and use only approved, encrypted, organisation-issued devices. Copying company data onto a personal drive creates risk even with the best intentions.

If you find an unknown drive, don't test it. Hand it to the security team.

lessons.title: Data Classification
lessons.narration:
Not all information carries the same risk, so it shouldn't get the same handling. That's what classification is for.

Public data is approved for anyone to see — published material, marketing content, information already in the open.

Internal data is for people inside the organisation. Process documents, internal announcements, routine operational information.

Confidential data is the material that causes real harm if exposed. Customer and employee personal data, financial records, contracts, credentials, system designs, network diagrams, anything covered by regulation.

For a utility, one category deserves particular care: engineering and design documentation. Network diagrams, control room layouts, equipment inventories, vendor lists, single-line diagrams. None of it is personal data, so it feels low-risk — but to an attacker planning an operation it is a map. In 2026 it was reported that roughly nineteen thousand documents relating to the Kudankulam nuclear project appeared on the dark web, apparently through a contractor rather than the plant itself: engineering drawings, control room layouts, supplier lists. The reactors were never touched. The blueprint still leaked.

Two practical rules. Know the classification of what you're handling before you send, share or store it. And apply the right controls — encryption, restricted access, approved channels only.

The most common breach isn't a hack. It's confidential information sent to the wrong recipient.

lessons.title: Report an Incident
lessons.narration:
Reporting is the single most valuable thing you can do, so let's make it easy.

When to report? Whenever something feels wrong. A suspicious email. A link you clicked and immediately regretted. A device that's gone missing. A login alert you didn't trigger. Unusual system behaviour. A stranger in a secured area. You don't need to be sure — uncertainty is exactly when to report.

How to report? Use the channels the organisation provides — the phishing report button, the helpdesk, or the security hotline. Report first, before trying to fix it yourself.

Who to contact? Know your security team's number before you need it. Save it in your phone today.

Attackers understand the value of delay. During the 2015 Ukraine grid attack, at the same moment they were opening breakers, they launched a flood of automated calls at the utility's customer service centre — jamming the lines so customers couldn't report the outage and operators couldn't work out what was happening. They also wiped the operators' workstations on the way out. Every one of those moves was designed to buy time by delaying detection. Fast reporting is how you take that time back.

Report fast, even if you think you made the mistake. Early reporting turns a potential crisis into a routine event. Nobody is punished for speaking up.

lessons.title: Insider Threats
lessons.narration:
Not every risk comes from outside. Some originate within — and most are not malicious at all.

Accidental insiders make ordinary human errors. An email to the wrong address. A file shared with a link set too widely. A laptop left in a taxi. No bad intent, real consequences.

Negligent insiders know the rules and work around them. Sharing a login to save time. Storing company files on a personal cloud account. Ignoring updates. Convenience wins, protection loses.

Malicious insiders are rare, but real — someone deliberately misusing legitimate access for personal gain or out of grievance.

A US rural water district discovered the risk in the plainest way possible. A former employee, whose remote access had never been revoked after he left, logged in and shut down the plant's cleaning and disinfection processes. No hacking was involved. No password was cracked. The account simply still worked. That is why the leavers process — collecting badges, disabling accounts, revoking VPN and vendor access on the last working day — is a security control and not an administrative formality.

What helps is straightforward. Take only the access you need. Follow the process even when it's slower. And if something genuinely concerns you, raise it discreetly with the security team.

lessons.title: Your Role in Security
lessons.narration:
Everything we've covered comes down to three habits.

Stay alert. Most attacks announce themselves if you're paying attention — the odd sender address, the unexpected urgency, the request that doesn't fit your normal process. Awareness costs seconds and saves everyone days.

Follow policies. They exist because someone, somewhere, learned the lesson the hard way. The VPN, the approved tools, the access requests, the classification rules — that's accumulated experience, not bureaucracy. And if a policy actively makes your job impossible, say so, so it can be fixed properly rather than quietly bypassed.

Speak up. Report what looks wrong. Ask when you're unsure. Challenge the unfamiliar face at a secured door. Tell us when you've clicked something you shouldn't have.

One image from the Ukraine attack captures this better than any statistic. An operator sat at his console and watched the mouse cursor move across the screen on its own — travelling to a breaker, selecting it, opening it. He grabbed the mouse and fought for control. He lost, and was then locked out of his own machine. But he was the detection system. No sensor raised that alarm. A person did, because he knew what normal looked like.

Technology stops a great deal. People stop the rest.

lessons.title: IT and OT Security
lessons.narration:
Welcome to the second part of this programme. Everything so far applied to any organisation anywhere. What follows is specific to us — to the business of generating and distributing electricity.

We'll be working with two worlds. IT — the systems that run the business: email, billing, HR, reporting. And OT, operational technology — the systems that run the grid: control rooms, substations, protection relays, SCADA.

Both matter. But they fail differently. When IT breaks, data is at risk. When OT breaks, power is at risk — and behind that sit hospitals, water pumping, traffic signals, and every home on our network.

This is no longer a hypothetical branch of security. Ukraine's grid has been attacked twice with real blackouts. India's regional and state load despatch centres have been found carrying implanted malware. In December 2025, more than thirty wind, solar and combined heat and power sites in Poland were hit in a single coordinated operation that physically damaged remote terminal units. OT attacks have moved from research papers to incident reports.

We'll also cover the CEA Cyber Security Regulations, which set out what every power utility in India must now do, and what that means for your daily work.

Whether you sit in an office or a switchyard, this section is for you.

lessons.title: What is OT Security?
lessons.narration:
Let's define both terms clearly, because this distinction shapes everything that follows.

IT — information technology — handles data. Emails, documents, databases, business applications. Its job is to keep information confidential, accurate and available.

OT — operational technology — handles the physical world. Sensors reading voltage, current and temperature. Controllers opening and closing breakers. Control room screens showing the live state of the network. Its job is to keep equipment running safely and predictably.

The simplest way to hold it: IT keeps data safe. OT keeps machines safe.

Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, was the moment this stopped being theoretical. It was the first malware built not to steal information but to break machinery — and it succeeded, destroying around a thousand centrifuges in Iran. What makes it instructive for us is the deception. While the equipment was being driven to destruction, the malware replayed earlier, normal-looking readings to the operators' screens. The people watching saw everything was fine. It wasn't. In OT, an attacker who controls your instrumentation controls your understanding of reality.

That changes the priority order. In IT we usually protect confidentiality first. In OT, availability and safety come first — because a control system that stops, or lies, has immediate physical consequences for equipment, for supply, and for people standing next to that equipment.

lessons.title: Why the Power Sector is a Target
lessons.narration:
Why would anyone attack a power utility? Three reasons.

First, we are critical infrastructure. Electricity underpins everything else — hospitals, water, transport, communications, industry. That makes the grid strategically valuable to attackers who want leverage rather than money.

Second, the impact is large-scale and immediate. An attack on many sectors means data is lost. An attack here means supply is lost, affecting an entire licence area at once.

Third, our systems are increasingly connected. Smart meters, remote substations, vendor support links, digital protection devices, IT and OT integration. Every connection adds capability — and a possible path inward.

The record is clear. December 2015: Ukraine, thirty substations opened remotely, two hundred and thirty thousand customers dark for up to six hours. December 2016: Kyiv, a fifth of the capital loses power to purpose-built malware that spoke industrial protocols natively. 2021 and 2022: security researchers report malware implanted in Indian regional and state load despatch centres — the bodies that balance the grid in real time. The stated goal was not disruption but pre-positioning: getting in quietly and waiting. December 2025: coordinated destructive attacks on Polish energy facilities.

Attackers range from criminal ransomware crews to state-sponsored teams who establish access and simply wait. India is squarely in scope — which is precisely why the regulations exist.

lessons.title: CEA Cyber Security Regulations
lessons.narration:
Which brings us to regulation.

India's Central Electricity Authority has issued the Cyber Security in Power Sector Regulations — a binding framework covering every entity in the power value chain: generation, transmission, distribution and load despatch.

They matter because they move cyber security from good practice to legal obligation. This is not guidance we may choose to adopt. It is a mandate, with defined roles, defined timelines, and consequences for non-compliance.

It's worth understanding why India legislated. In September 2019, malware was found on a computer on the administrative network of the Kudankulam nuclear plant, reaching a facility most people assumed was untouchable. From 2020 onwards, researchers documented sustained intrusions into load despatch centres across the country. The regulations are a direct response to that evidence: the state concluded that the security of the national grid was too important to leave to each operator's discretion.

The regulations span governance — who is accountable. Technical controls — how systems must be protected and separated. Incident reporting — what must be reported, to whom, and how quickly. Supply chain — what we require of our vendors. And people — training and awareness for everyone who touches these systems.

That last point is why you're watching this. Awareness training is a regulatory requirement, and your completion is part of our evidence.

lessons.title: CEA Key Requirements
lessons.narration:
Five requirements worth recognising.

One: appoint a CISO. A designated, accountable senior officer for cyber security, with a nominated alternate, both notified to the authorities. Accountability is named, not shared.

Two: conduct cyber audits. Regular assessments by empanelled auditors covering both IT and OT, with findings tracked to closure.

Three: network segmentation. Operational systems must be separated from business networks and from the internet, with controlled and monitored crossing points.

Four: incident reporting within six hours of noticing a cyber incident.

Five: employee awareness training, refreshed regularly, with records maintained.

Focus on that six-hour clock, because it's the one that touches you. Six hours is not long. It has to cover you noticing something, telling the security team, the team confirming it's real, gathering enough detail to describe it, and filing with the authorities. If you sit on an observation until the end of your shift, you have consumed most of the window before anyone else even knows. In the Ukraine attack the operators recognised something was wrong within minutes — and even then the attackers had jammed the phone lines to slow the alarm. Speed of reporting is a control in its own right.

Four of these are the organisation's job. The fifth, and that clock, depend on you.

lessons.title: IT vs OT: Key Differences
lessons.narration:
Understanding the differences explains why OT carries its own rules.

Lifespan. An office laptop is replaced every three to five years. A protection relay or controller may run for fifteen or twenty. Much of our OT estate predates modern security design entirely.

Patching. IT systems patch monthly, often automatically. OT patching needs a planned outage, vendor validation and formal approval — because an untested update on a live control system can trip equipment.

Priority. IT protects data first. OT protects availability and safety first.

Protocols. OT speaks industrial languages — Modbus, DNP3, IEC 61850 — many designed decades ago with no authentication and no encryption, on the assumption that the network was isolated.

Recovery differs most of all. When IT is hit, you rebuild from backups. When OT is hit, you may have nothing to rebuild onto. In Ukraine the attackers overwrote the firmware on the serial-to-Ethernet converters at the substations, bricking them permanently. The utility could no longer operate those breakers remotely at all. For months afterwards, engineers drove to substations and switched them by hand. You cannot restore damaged field hardware from a backup tape.

So never apply IT habits to OT systems. Follow the OT procedure.

lessons.title: SCADA and ICS Security
lessons.narration:
SCADA and industrial control systems are the nervous system of our operations. Protecting them rests on three practices.

Restrict remote access. Every connection into a control environment must be authorised, individually attributed, multi-factor authenticated, time-limited and recorded. This applies most strictly to vendors: remote support sessions are requested, approved, supervised while active, and closed afterwards. Standing, always-on vendor access is precisely how attackers get in.

Patch regularly — the OT way. Through the change process, in a maintenance window, tested first, with a rollback plan ready. Never ad hoc on a live system.

Monitor for anomalies. Unexpected commands, new devices, unusual traffic, logins at odd hours, a setting that changed without a work order.

The Polish incident of December 2025 shows how current this is. Attackers got in through internet-facing edge devices — routers and gateways sitting at the network perimeter, running out-of-date firmware. From there they deployed wiper malware and damaged remote terminal units across more than thirty renewable and combined heat and power sites. Supply held, but the operational damage was physical and real. The lesson is unglamorous: the forgotten box at the edge of the network, the one nobody has patched because nobody remembers owning it, is where these attacks start.

If it doesn't match known, authorised activity, treat it as an incident until proven otherwise.

lessons.title: Network Segmentation
lessons.narration:
Segmentation is the single most effective OT control we have. The principle is simple: IT and OT do not talk to each other directly.

Between them sits a DMZ — a buffer zone. Data that operations needs to share with the business is published into the DMZ, and business systems read it from there. Neither side reaches across.

Firewalls enforce that boundary, permitting only specific, approved traffic in a controlled direction. Everything else is denied by default. The most sensitive systems are isolated further still.

Two incidents show both sides of this. At Kudankulam in 2019, malware reached the administrative network — but the operational systems were genuinely separated, and the reactors were never affected. Segmentation did its job. Contrast that with Colonial Pipeline in 2021: the ransomware hit the IT side, not the control systems, yet the company shut the pipeline down anyway — because they could not be certain the separation would hold, and could not risk finding out. Good segmentation contains an incident. Uncertain segmentation forces you to shut down out of caution.

What this means for you is short but important. Never create your own bridge. Don't connect a laptop to both networks. Don't plug a phone, dongle or personal modem into an OT switch. Don't set up an unapproved wireless link or remote-access tool.

One shortcut can undo the entire design.

lessons.title: Incident Response for OT
lessons.narration:
If something looks wrong in an operational system, four steps.

Detect. Trust your instruments and your instincts. A reading that doesn't match physical reality. A command nobody issued. A device behaving oddly. An unfamiliar login. You know normal better than any tool does.

Isolate. Contain the affected system — but only through the approved procedure and with operational authority. In OT, disconnecting the wrong thing can do more damage than the attack. Safety and grid stability come first, so coordinate. Never act alone.

Report. Immediately, to the CISO office. The regulation gives us six hours to notify the authorities, and that clock starts when the incident is noticed.

Restore safely. Recovery is planned, sequenced and verified by the response team, once the system is confirmed clean.

Norsk Hydro is the model worth copying. They isolated fast, refused to pay, ran their plants manually where they could, and communicated openly with staff, customers and press throughout. It still cost them around seventy million dollars — but they kept operating and kept their reputation. The difference between a bad day and a catastrophe is usually the quality of the response, not the sophistication of the attack.

lessons.title: Your Role in OT Security
lessons.narration:
Three commitments to close this section.

Follow access controls. Use your own credentials, never anyone else's. Request only the access your role genuinely needs. Don't prop open doors to substations or control rooms, don't share badges, and never leave a logged-in operator console unattended. And when a colleague or contractor leaves, make sure their access goes with them — a water utility in the United States was sabotaged by a former employee whose remote login simply still worked.

Report anomalies. You are a detection layer no sensor replaces. An odd reading, an unexpected visitor, an engineer whose work order doesn't quite fit, a device that appeared without explanation — report it. Being wrong costs a phone call. Staying quiet can cost a great deal more.

Remember the Ukrainian operator watching his cursor move by itself. Every technical control in that utility had already been passed. He was the alarm. In our control rooms and substations, so are you.

Complete your cyber training. Not simply because a regulation requires it, but because it keeps the first two habits current as the threats change.

Reliable power depends on secure systems. Secure systems depend on you.

lessons.title: Key Takeaways
lessons.narration:
Let's close with what's worth carrying out of this session.

Think before you click. Verify the sender, hover over links, and treat urgency as a warning sign rather than an instruction. A single opened attachment started the first blackout in history caused by a cyberattack.

Use strong, unique passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere it's offered. One reused password on one forgotten account shut down a pipeline serving half a continent.

Protect your devices and your data. Lock your screen, use the VPN, never plug in unknown USB drives — one carried malware across an air gap and destroyed a thousand machines — and handle confidential information through approved channels only.

And report anything suspicious immediately, even, and especially, when you think the mistake was yours. In almost every case we've looked at, earlier reporting would have meant a smaller incident.

None of this requires you to become a security expert. It asks for a few seconds of attention at the right moments, and the confidence to ask a question when something feels off.

You now have both. Thank you for your time — and welcome to the team that keeps this organisation secure.

lessons.title: Quiz Prompt
lessons.narration:
That's the end of the training. Before you go, let's find out what stayed
with you.

What follows is a short assessment: ten questions drawn from everything we've
covered across both parts of this programme. Each question has one correct
answer. There's no time limit, so read each one properly before you choose.

Get seven or more right and you pass, and your certificate is issued straight
away. Score under seven and you're welcome to try again. That's all that
happens, nothing else changes. Your completion of this training is already
recorded, and the awareness requirement is met either way. The certificate is
the extra step, not the whole point, so there's nothing to be nervous about.

This isn't a memory test. It's a check on whether the habits we've talked
about will be there when you actually need them: the pause before the click,
the second look at the sender, the phone call you make rather than the one
you take.

Take your time, read carefully, and good luck.

questions.prompt: Why does an attacker want the ordinary data you handle day to day?
options: Because most of it is classified at the highest level
Because it is usually worth more than the organisation's money
Because it can be sold, held to ransom, or used as a way into something bigger
Because it is the only thing not protected by the firewall
questions.explains: Almost everything has value to somebody: customer records, financial data, your own credentials. To an attacker each is either something to sell, something to hold hostage, or a door into something larger.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the consequences of a breach is accurate?
options: The damage is almost always limited to the account that was compromised
One compromised account can shut down services, expose personal data and trigger regulatory action
The main cost is replacing the hardware that was affected
Consequences are financial only, and are usually covered by insurance
questions.explains: The consequences are not contained to the account. A single compromise can halt services people depend on, expose data belonging to customers and colleagues, and cost a reputation that took decades to build.

questions.prompt: Security at work is often described as the organisation's problem. Why is that incomplete?
options: Because the organisation has no legal duty to protect your data
Because home devices are always more secure than work ones
Because attackers only ever target organisations, never individuals
The same habits protect your own bank account, photos and identity
questions.explains: The habits are the same in both places. Good security at work makes you safer everywhere, which is why it is worth the seconds it costs.

questions.prompt: Phishing remains the most common way attacks begin. Why is it so effective?
options: It does not look like an attack — it looks like an ordinary email
It exploits a flaw in email software that cannot be patched
It only targets people who have never had security training
It always arrives from an address nobody in the company recognises
questions.explains: There is no technical trick to spot. It arrives looking like work, which is why the defence is a habit rather than a tool.

questions.prompt: A message displays the name of a colleague you know well. What does that establish?
options: That the message genuinely came from that colleague's account
Very little — the display name is chosen by the sender and the real address may be quite different
That the message passed the organisation's spam filtering
That the sending domain has been verified by the mail provider
questions.explains: A display name is decoration. The address behind it is often subtly wrong: an extra letter, a different domain, a public mail service where a company address should be. Read the address, not the name.

questions.prompt: Phishing messages very often insist you act within the hour. Why?
options: Because the attacker's access to the fake site genuinely expires
Because mail systems delete suspicious messages after an hour
Because urgent messages are more likely to bypass spam filters
Urgency is designed to stop you thinking and start you clicking
questions.explains: The pressure is the attack. Genuine business rarely arrives with a countdown attached, so treat urgency as a warning sign rather than an instruction.

questions.prompt: What does hovering over a link before clicking actually tell you?
options: Whether the destination site is currently online
Whether the link has been scanned by antivirus
Where the link really goes, which is often not what the text on screen says
Whether the sender intended you to click it
questions.explains: The visible text and the real destination are two different things and are often deliberately different. Hover first, read the domain, click second.

questions.prompt: You get an invoice attachment from a supplier you have never ordered from. What is the safest response?
options: Do not open it, and report it
Open it to find out which order it refers to
Forward it to the finance team to identify
Open it, but only after disabling macros
questions.explains: Unexpected invoices and delivery notices are among the most common ways malware arrives. Opening it to identify it is doing the attacker's work. Report it instead.

questions.prompt: A document asks you to enable content or enable editing before it will display. What does that usually mean?
options: It is trying to run macros, and that prompt is the attack
The file was created in a newer version of the software
Your licence has expired and needs to be refreshed
The document is protected and requires your password
questions.explains: That prompt exists to get you to switch off the protection that is stopping the file running code. A genuine document does not need it to be readable.

questions.prompt: How many red flags should it take before you stop and report a message?
options: Three or more, otherwise reports become too frequent
One is enough to justify a second look, and two together mean stop
Only when you are certain the message is malicious
Only if the message asks for money directly
questions.explains: You do not need certainty. One flag deserves a closer look; two together mean stop and report. Nobody is penalised for a report that turns out to be nothing.

questions.prompt: A message claiming to be from your bank links to a completely unrelated domain. What is that?
options: Normal, because banks use third-party marketing providers
Evidence the message was forwarded by a colleague
A sign the link has been shortened for convenience
A mismatch between sender and destination, which is a classic phishing sign
questions.explains: The destination should match the sender. A message that claims one identity and links somewhere unrelated is telling you what it is.

questions.prompt: Which matters more in a password: length or symbol complexity?
options: Complexity, because symbols defeat automated cracking
Neither, as long as the password is changed every month
Length — a long passphrase of unrelated words beats a short string of symbols
Complexity, because length is limited by most websites anyway
questions.explains: Length beats complexity, and it is easier to remember. Aim for twelve to sixteen characters or more; a few unrelated words does it.

questions.prompt: Why is reusing one password across accounts the most damaging habit?
options: Because websites can detect reuse and lock the account
Because reused passwords expire faster than unique ones
When any one site is breached, attackers immediately try that pair everywhere else
Because it makes the password easier to guess directly
questions.explains: Breaches happen constantly, and leaked credentials are replayed against every other service within hours. One reused password can unlock a dozen accounts.

questions.prompt: Is using a password manager a shortcut that weakens security?
options: Yes, because all the passwords sit in one place
No — it is the practical way to have a strong, unique password everywhere
Yes, because it removes the need to remember anything
It makes no difference either way to account security
questions.explains: It generates and remembers a unique strong password per site so you only recall one master passphrase. That is not cutting a corner; it is the only realistic way to do this properly.

questions.prompt: The IT helpdesk phones and asks for your password to fix an account problem. What do you do?
options: Give it, since the helpdesk is authorised to hold credentials
Give it, but change the password immediately afterwards
Give only the first half, so it cannot be used on its own
Refuse — no legitimate team ever needs your password
questions.explains: Nobody legitimate needs your password: not a colleague, not IT, not anyone who asks. A request for it is the attack, whoever appears to be asking.

questions.prompt: What does multi-factor authentication actually protect against?
options: A stolen password being enough on its own
Your password being guessed in the first place
Malware already running on your laptop
Phishing emails reaching your inbox
questions.explains: It does not stop the password being stolen. It makes the theft useless: without the second factor in your pocket, the password alone gets nobody in.

questions.prompt: Which second factor is preferable where you have the choice?
options: A code sent by text message
An authenticator app or a hardware security key
A memorable security question
A second password kept separately
questions.explains: SMS codes can be intercepted or redirected. An authenticator app or a hardware key is materially stronger, and it is usually just a setting.

questions.prompt: Your phone buzzes repeatedly with approval requests you did not trigger. What is happening?
options: Somebody already has your password and is hoping you will tap approve to stop the buzzing
The authenticator app has lost sync and needs re-registering
Your account is being migrated to a new sign-in system
The network is retrying a request that failed earlier
questions.explains: An unexpected prompt can only be generated by somebody entering your password. This is called MFA fatigue and it works on people who just want the noise to stop. Deny it, then report it.

questions.prompt: What are the two factors in multi-factor authentication?
options: Something you know and somewhere you are
Two things you know, kept separately
A password and the answer to a security question
Something you know and something you have
questions.explains: Your password is something you know; your phone, app or key is something you have. The strength comes from the two being different kinds of thing.

questions.prompt: Which part of a web address deserves the most attention?
options: The words at the very end of the address
Whether the address begins with www
The domain name immediately before the first single slash
The length of the address overall
questions.explains: Everything after the domain is chosen by whoever owns it. Attackers put reassuring words in the path precisely because people read left to right and stop early.

questions.prompt: A pop-up warns that your device is infected and offers a fix. What should you do?
options: Click the scan button to check whether it is true
Close the tab without interacting with the pop-up
Click the close button inside the pop-up window
Install the offered tool, then remove it afterwards
questions.explains: Both the warning and its buttons are bait, including the one that looks like close. Shut the tab itself and, if you are unsure, report it.

questions.prompt: Why is free software from an unofficial download site a risk?
options: Unofficial sites are always slower to download from
The software will be an older version than the official one
It breaches the licence but is otherwise technically safe
The installer is a convenient way to deliver something else alongside it
questions.explains: Repackaged installers are a standard delivery method for malware. Free rarely is; get software from the official source or through IT.

questions.prompt: Social engineering works by exploiting which human tendencies?
options: Helpfulness, respect for authority, and the wish to avoid conflict
Carelessness and lack of training
Greed and dishonesty
Inexperience with computers
questions.explains: It targets instincts that normally serve you well, which is why being a decent colleague is not protection. Verification is.

questions.prompt: Someone calls claiming to be a vendor engineer with a plausible, detailed story. What is that technique called?
options: Tailgating — following someone into a restricted place
Baiting — leaving something tempting to be picked up
Pretexting — an invented backstory to justify the request
Shoulder surfing — reading information over someone's shoulder
questions.explains: Pretexting is the invented context that makes the request seem reasonable. The detail is what sells it, and detail is easy to research.

questions.prompt: Why do attackers so often impersonate a senior executive?
options: Because people hesitate to question someone senior
Because executive accounts have no multi-factor authentication
Because executives are the only staff with system access
Because their email addresses are the easiest to guess
questions.explains: The borrowed authority is the point: it discourages the one step that would defeat the attack, which is checking.

questions.prompt: What is the single defence that works against every social engineering approach?
options: Ask the caller for more details to test their story
Ask them to put the request in writing by email
Check whether the caller ID matches a known number
Verify independently — hang up and call back on a number you already trust
questions.explains: Verification through a channel you chose defeats the whole family of attacks. Asking for detail invites a better story; caller ID and email can both be faked. A genuine request survives a call back.

questions.prompt: A caller knows your address and your last transaction. What does that prove?
options: That the caller has legitimate access to your account
That the call originated from inside your bank's network
Nothing — those details come from breaches, social media or an earlier call
That the caller is who they say they are, but may still be mistaken
questions.explains: A handful of real details is cheap to obtain and is used precisely because it makes everything after it sound true.

questions.prompt: Your phone shows your bank's real published number. Can the call be trusted?
options: Yes, a displayed number cannot be faked by a caller
No — caller ID is trivially spoofed and proves nothing at all
Yes, provided the caller does not ask for your full password
Only if the call arrives during the bank's opening hours
questions.explains: Spoofing a number takes no effort. The number on your screen is a claim, not evidence. Hang up and call back on a number you already trust.

questions.prompt: A text says a parcel could not be delivered and links to a page to rearrange it. What is that?
options: Smishing — phishing by text message
Vishing — phishing by voice call
A legitimate notification from the courier
A spam message with no security implication
questions.explains: Failed delivery, blocked payment and pending refund are the three most common smishing pretexts, because almost everybody is expecting one of them.

questions.prompt: A caller asks you to install remote-access software so they can fix a problem. What should you do?
options: Install it, but disconnect as soon as they finish
Install it only if they can name your manager
Ask them to email the software instead
Refuse, end the call, and report it
questions.explains: Handing over remote access hands over everything the account can reach. No genuine support process begins with an unsolicited call asking for it.

questions.prompt: How does ransomware usually get in?
options: By exploiting a flaw in the electricity supply to servers
Through the organisation's public website being defaced
Through a phishing attachment, a malicious link, or a compromised remote-access account
By physically breaking into the server room
questions.explains: It arrives quietly through ordinary routes, which is why the everyday habits in this course are what actually prevent it.

questions.prompt: Your organisation has complete, tested, offline backups. Why is ransomware still a serious problem?
options: Restoring from backup is slow but the risk is otherwise handled
Attackers usually copy the data out before encrypting it, and threaten to publish
Backups are normally encrypted by the ransomware as well
Payment is still required to obtain the decryption key
questions.explains: This is double extortion. Backups solve availability; they do nothing about disclosure. Even a perfect restore leaves the second threat intact.

questions.prompt: What is the realistic timescale for recovering from a serious ransomware incident?
options: A few hours, once the ransom decision is made
Minutes, if backups are held offsite
Days to weeks, with operations halted in the meantime
It depends entirely on whether the ransom is paid
questions.explains: Systems stop, operations halt and teams sit idle. Recovery is measured in days and weeks, which is why prevention is dramatically cheaper.

questions.prompt: What does ransomware do first once it is inside?
options: Displays the ransom demand immediately
Deletes the operating system so the machine will not restart
Sends a copy of itself to everyone in your address book
Begins encrypting everything it can reach, including shared drives
questions.explains: The demand appears after the damage is done. By the time you see it, it has already reached whatever the account could reach.

questions.prompt: Files are renaming themselves with a strange extension. What is your first action?
options: Disconnect from the network but leave the machine running
Shut the machine down immediately to stop the encryption
Run a full antivirus scan before telling anyone
Close the application and see whether it stops on its own
questions.explains: Disconnect, but do not power off. Pulling the cable and switching off Wi-Fi limits the spread to shared drives; shutting down feels decisive and destroys evidence that exists only in memory.

questions.prompt: Why should you not power off a machine you suspect is running ransomware?
options: Powering off can corrupt the encrypted files permanently
Evidence the response team needs lives in memory and is lost on shutdown
The machine may not restart afterwards
It triggers the ransomware to delete files immediately
questions.explains: Memory holds the material that lets the response team understand what happened and how far it went. Disconnect instead.

questions.prompt: You worry you may have caused the infection. Should that change when you report?
options: Yes, gather evidence first so the report is accurate
No — report immediately, because minutes limit the damage and nobody is penalised for raising the alarm
Yes, tell your manager privately before the security team
Yes, wait until the end of your shift to avoid disruption
questions.explains: Delay is the only thing that makes it worse. Fast reporting is what turns a potential crisis into a routine event, and it is explicitly not held against anybody.

questions.prompt: Who decides whether a ransom is paid?
options: The person whose machine was infected, since they know the files
Whoever holds the corporate cryptocurrency wallet
The team leader on shift at the time
Not you — it is not a decision for the person who found it, and never one to make alone
questions.explains: Payment funds the next attack and guarantees nothing. The decision is not yours to carry; disconnect, report, and let the response team work.

questions.prompt: Someone with full hands follows you through a badge-controlled door. What should you do?
options: Let the door close and ask them to badge in
Hold the door — refusing would be rude and they clearly work here
Hold the door, then mention it to security afterwards
Let the door close, then hold it open once they show you a badge
questions.explains: Tailgating works precisely because stopping it feels rude, and full hands are a standard pretext. Holding the door is not politeness, it is an access-control bypass — and showing a badge is not the same as badging in.

questions.prompt: Why is a clean desk described as a security control?
options: Because clutter slows down the cleaning staff
Because paper documents are the most common way malware spreads
Papers and notes left out are readable by everyone who passes, including visitors and contractors
Because insurers require it before covering an office
questions.explains: Documents, notes with credentials, unlocked drawers — all of it is available to anyone walking past. Lock papers away and lock your screen every single time you step away.

questions.prompt: Why does the organisation ask you to wear your badge visibly?
options: It allows security cameras to identify you automatically
It is required by fire regulations for headcount
It is how colleagues know you belong, and how an unfamiliar face becomes noticeable
It stops the badge being cloned while in your pocket
questions.explains: Visible badges make the exception visible. If everyone wears one, somebody without one stands out — which is the whole mechanism.

questions.prompt: You see an unfamiliar person in a restricted area. What is the right response?
options: Assume they have been escorted in by someone else
Say nothing unless they touch equipment
Follow them at a distance to see what they do
Ask who they are, or report it
questions.explains: Asking costs a moment of mild awkwardness. Assuming somebody else has checked is exactly what an intruder is relying on.

questions.prompt: When should the VPN be connected while working remotely?
options: Before you start working, and for the whole session
Only when opening confidential documents
Only when connected to a network you do not control
Only when the helpdesk asks you to
questions.explains: Connect first, then work. It encrypts your traffic and keeps access to company systems controlled; switching it on selectively defeats the point.

questions.prompt: Which of these actually matters for securing your home Wi-Fi?
options: Hiding the network name so it is not broadcast
Changing the default router password and using WPA2 or WPA3
Changing the network name to something anonymous
Restricting the number of devices that may connect
questions.explains: The default password and the encryption standard are what an attacker actually has to get past. Hiding the name stops nobody. Your home network is now part of the organisation's attack surface.

questions.prompt: You are working in a café. What is the overlooked risk beyond the network?
options: People nearby who can see your screen or hear your call
The café's electricity supply damaging your laptop
Your laptop overheating in a warm room
Losing connection halfway through saving a file
questions.explains: Shoulder surfing needs no technology at all. Be aware of who can see and hear; confidential conversations deserve a closed door.

questions.prompt: What is the main technical risk on an open public network?
options: The network being slower than a mobile connection
Your device being visible in the venue's guest list
Automatic installation of software by the venue
Interception — somebody nearby watching unencrypted traffic or sitting between you and the site
questions.explains: On an open network you have no idea who else is on it. Interception and man-in-the-middle positioning are the real risks, and the VPN is the answer to both.

questions.prompt: You see two networks: "Airport_WiFi" and "Airport WiFi Free". Which is safe?
options: Whichever has the stronger signal
The one requiring a password, since open networks are the risk
Neither, until you confirm the exact name with staff
Either, as long as you only browse and do not sign in anywhere
questions.explains: A fake hotspot named to look official is a standard trick, and a password on it proves nothing — the attacker chose the password. Verify the exact name with staff.

questions.prompt: Which is safer: the café's Wi-Fi with a VPN, or your own mobile hotspot?
options: The café Wi-Fi, because the VPN makes it equivalent
Your own mobile hotspot, because you control it
The café Wi-Fi, because mobile data is unencrypted
They carry exactly the same risk
questions.explains: A VPN on public Wi-Fi is good. A network you set up yourself is better, and is the recommendation whenever you have the choice.

questions.prompt: Which tasks should wait until you are on a trusted connection or VPN?
options: Anything involving a web browser
Only tasks that require a password
Banking, payments and confidential work
Any task that takes longer than a few minutes
questions.explains: Sensitive tasks are the ones worth an attacker's attention. Everything else is lower stakes, but the VPN costs nothing to leave on.

questions.prompt: You find an unlabelled USB drive in the car park. What should you do?
options: Plug it into an isolated machine to find the owner
Hand it to the security team without plugging it in anywhere
Scan it with antivirus first, then look for a name
Leave it where it is in case the owner returns
questions.explains: Dropped drives are a real technique that relies on exactly this curiosity. Some carry malware; others imitate a keyboard and type commands the instant they are connected, which no scan will catch.

questions.prompt: Why can an antivirus scan miss a malicious USB device entirely?
options: Some devices pretend to be a keyboard and type commands rather than storing files
Antivirus cannot read removable media at all
The malware is hidden in the device's serial number
Scanning only works after the files have been copied off
questions.explains: There is no file to scan. The device is recognised as input hardware and starts typing the moment it is connected.

questions.prompt: Copying company files to your own USB drive to finish work at home. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing, provided the files are deleted afterwards
Nothing, as long as the drive stays in your possession
It is only a problem if the drive is not encrypted
Once data leaves controlled systems it cannot be tracked, protected or wiped
questions.explains: Good intentions do not change the outcome. This is the textbook negligent insider action: the rule is known, convenience wins, and the data is now somewhere nobody can account for.

questions.prompt: If removable media genuinely has to be used, what does the policy require?
options: Any device, provided it is scanned first
Any new device still in its packaging
An approved, issued device, encrypted, and scanned before use
A device belonging to a colleague you trust
questions.explains: Approved and issued means it can be accounted for; encrypted means a loss is not a breach. Both matter, and scanning alone covers neither.

questions.prompt: Internal process documents and routine announcements are classified as what?
options: Internal
Public
Confidential
Unclassified
questions.explains: Not damaging on its own, but not for outside eyes either. Public is approved for anyone; confidential is the material that causes real harm if exposed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is confidential rather than internal?
options: An internal announcement about office opening hours
Employee personal data covered by regulation
A published marketing brochure
The company's standard process documentation
questions.explains: Customer and employee personal data, financial records, contracts, credentials and system designs are the material that causes real harm if exposed.

questions.prompt: What causes the most breaches in practice?
options: Attackers breaking through technical defences
Stolen or lost laptops
Malware delivered through software vulnerabilities
Confidential information sent to the wrong recipient
questions.explains: The most common breach is not a hack. It is a mistyped address, a reply-all, or a link shared more widely than intended — which is why knowing the classification before you send matters.

questions.prompt: You clicked a link an hour ago and nothing seems to have happened. What now?
options: Watch for unusual behaviour and report only if something appears
Run a virus scan and report only if it finds something
Change your password quietly and move on
Report it now, even though you are not sure anything went wrong
questions.explains: Uncertainty is exactly when to report. Waiting for symptoms wastes the window in which damage can still be limited, and nobody is penalised for raising the alarm.

questions.prompt: Which of these is worth reporting?
options: Only incidents that have clearly caused damage
All of these — a suspicious email, a missing device, a login alert you did not trigger
Only incidents involving confidential data
Only incidents you can explain fully
questions.explains: You do not need to be sure and you do not need to understand it. If something feels wrong, that is the threshold.

questions.prompt: What should you do before trying to fix a suspected incident yourself?
options: Report it first
Take screenshots and write up what happened
Isolate the machine and run a full scan
Check with a colleague whether they have seen the same thing
questions.explains: Report first. Well-meant fixes can destroy evidence and cost time that matters, and the response team would rather start early than tidy up after.

questions.prompt: When is the right time to find out your security team's contact number?
options: When an incident happens, from the intranet
When your manager circulates it
Today, before you need it
It is not needed if you can email the helpdesk
questions.explains: Looking it up mid-incident costs the minutes that matter. Save it in your phone now.

questions.prompt: A colleague shares their login with a new starter whose account is not ready. How is that best described?
options: Sensible teamwork, since the work still needs doing
A malicious insider action
Not a security matter, since neither intends harm
A negligent insider action: the rule is known and worked around
questions.explains: Negligent, not malicious — and that distinction matters because most insider risk looks exactly like this. The consequence is that two people now act under one identity and nothing afterwards can tell them apart.

questions.prompt: Which kind of insider risk is the most common?
options: Accidental — ordinary human error with no bad intent
Malicious — deliberate misuse for personal gain
Negligent — knowingly working around the rules
External actors using stolen insider credentials
questions.explains: An email to the wrong address, a file shared too widely, a laptop left in a taxi. No bad intent, real consequences, and by far the largest share.

questions.prompt: What does taking only the access your role needs actually protect against?
options: Your account being locked for inactivity
Colleagues seeing what you have access to
The damage any single compromised account or mistake can cause
The need to complete access review paperwork
questions.explains: Least privilege limits the blast radius of both an honest mistake and a stolen credential. It is not about trust; it is about consequences.

questions.prompt: You notice a colleague copying unusual volumes of data. What is the right step?
options: Confront them directly to hear their explanation
Raise it discreetly with the security team
Mention it informally to other colleagues first
Do nothing unless you see it happen a second time
questions.explains: Discreet is the operative word: you may be wrong, and the point is to have it looked at properly rather than to accuse anybody.

questions.prompt: A security policy makes a routine part of your job impossible. What should you do?
options: Work around it and mention it if anyone asks
Follow it exactly and accept the work will not get done
Ask a colleague how they get around it
Say so, so it can be fixed properly rather than quietly bypassed
questions.explains: Policies are accumulated experience, but a policy nobody can follow gets bypassed silently, which is worse than either following or changing it. Say so and get it fixed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference in what is at risk when IT fails versus when OT fails?
options: Both put data at risk, but OT affects more records
IT failures are always more expensive to recover from
When IT breaks data is at risk; when OT breaks power is at risk
OT failures are contained to the site where they happen
questions.explains: Behind an OT failure sit hospitals, water pumping, traffic signals and every home on the network. Both matter, but they fail differently.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest way to hold the difference between IT and OT?
options: IT keeps data safe; OT keeps machines safe
IT is office software; OT is anything on a factory floor
IT is modern systems; OT is legacy systems
IT is owned by the business; OT is owned by the vendor
questions.explains: IT handles information — emails, documents, databases. OT handles the physical world: sensors reading voltage, controllers opening breakers, screens showing the live state of the network.

questions.prompt: In IT we usually protect confidentiality first. What comes first in OT?
options: Confidentiality, for the same reasons as IT
Availability and safety
Integrity of the historian records
Regulatory reporting obligations
questions.explains: A control system that stops, or misbehaves, has immediate physical consequences for equipment, for supply, and for people standing next to that equipment. The priority order genuinely inverts.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an OT device rather than an IT one?
options: A protection relay that opens a breaker
A database server holding customer records
The corporate email gateway
A laptop used for billing reports
questions.explains: OT is the equipment that senses and acts on the physical world. If it measures voltage or moves something, it is OT.

questions.prompt: Why does the priority order matter in practice?
options: It changes which team is responsible for the budget
It determines which systems are audited first
It only affects how incidents are documented afterwards
It means a control that is correct for IT can be the wrong action in OT
questions.explains: Same discipline, very different stakes — which is why the OT procedure exists and why IT habits should not be carried across.

questions.prompt: Why is the power sector attractive to attackers seeking leverage rather than money?
options: Power utilities hold more personal data than other sectors
Electricity underpins hospitals, water, transport, communications and industry
Power companies are less likely to have security teams
Grid systems are easier to breach than banking systems
questions.explains: Being critical infrastructure is the point: the leverage comes from what stops when the power does.

questions.prompt: How does the impact of an attack here differ from most other sectors?
options: The financial loss is smaller but takes longer to recover
Only the operator's own equipment is affected
Supply is lost, not just data — affecting an entire licence area at once
The impact is identical, but reporting requirements are stricter
questions.explains: That immediate, wide impact also generates enormous pressure to restore at any cost, which is exactly the leverage an attacker is looking for.

questions.prompt: Which trend has increased the number of possible ways in?
options: Smart meters, remote substations, vendor links and IT/OT integration
The replacement of analogue meters with mechanical ones
The reduction in the number of substations
Consolidation of control rooms into fewer sites
questions.explains: Every connection adds capability and a possible path inward. The actors range from ransomware crews to state-sponsored teams who establish access and simply wait.

questions.prompt: What status do the CEA Cyber Security Regulations have?
options: Voluntary guidance that utilities may choose to adopt
An international standard adopted by agreement
An internal policy set by each utility's own board
A binding legal mandate with defined roles, timelines and consequences
questions.explains: They move cyber security from good practice to legal obligation across the whole power value chain.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the power value chain do the regulations cover?
options: Generation and transmission only
Distribution companies only
Generation, transmission, distribution and load despatch
Only entities that operate across more than one state
questions.explains: Every entity in the chain is in scope, which is why this applies whatever part of the business you sit in.

questions.prompt: Why does awareness training appear in a regulation at all?
options: Because regulators require a minimum training budget
Because training and awareness are a stated requirement, and completion is evidence of compliance
Because insurers will not otherwise provide cover
It does not — training is organisational goodwill
questions.explains: Your completion record is part of how the organisation demonstrates compliance. That is why this is not optional.

questions.prompt: Within how long must a cyber incident be reported to the designated authorities?
options: Twenty-four hours from being noticed
Six hours from being noticed
Seventy-two hours, in line with data protection rules
By the end of the working day on which it was found
questions.explains: Six hours is a tight clock, and it starts when the incident is noticed — which means your report to the security team has to be immediate, not at the end of your shift.

questions.prompt: What does the regulation require regarding accountability for cyber security?
options: A cyber security committee drawn from every department
Shared accountability across the senior leadership team
An external consultant retained on permanent contract
A designated CISO and a nominated alternate, both notified to the authorities
questions.explains: Accountability is named, not shared. A designated senior officer and a named alternate, both notified.

questions.prompt: What must cyber audits cover, and who performs them?
options: IT systems only, by the internal audit team
OT systems only, by the equipment vendor
Both IT and OT, by empanelled auditors, with findings tracked to closure
Whichever systems the utility selects, by any qualified firm
questions.explains: Both estates, by empanelled auditors, and the findings have to be followed through rather than filed.

questions.prompt: Of the five key requirements, which one depends directly on you?
options: Employee awareness training, and the immediacy that makes the six-hour clock achievable
Appointing a CISO
Commissioning the cyber audit
